newsitem.title: CHINA: China share issues likely to exceed demand -expert.
newsitem.headline: China share issues likely to exceed demand -expert.

text.p: New share issues on China's two stock markets in 1997 are likely to exceed demand, with activity by individual investors expected to be much reduced from last year, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

The newspaper quoted He Qiang, an assistant professor at the Central University of Finance and Economics as saying an over-supply of issues this year would create a buyers' market, in sharp contrast to the situation in 1996.
The securities authorities set a new share issue quota at the end of last year of 10 billion yuan, double the previous quota.
"Yet demand for stocks was expected to wither after the market cooled down from excessive speculation," the newspaper quoted He as saying.
The authorities stepped in to rein in the markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen in mid-December after months of feverish trading that pushed prices up dramatically.
Individual investors were last year encouraged by two interest rate cuts to remove funds from their bank accounts to invest in the stock markets.
But He said the impact of the interest rate cuts was fading, and people were becoming less likely to withdraw their money from bank deposits in search of high returns.
Institutional buyers will also show less interest in the stock markets this year, he said.

He predicted the futures markets, which have been sharply curtailed in the past two years due to Beijing's impatience with the casino-like gambling on minor products on some exchanges, would recover to some extent in 1997.
The stock markets were also expected to suffer from the crackdown on the use of illegal funds to buy shares, particularly the use of credit, He said.

"Although there are no precise figures for illegal funds in the stock market, including overdrafts, corporation loans and banking deposits, the illegal money contributed significantly to the overheated market last year," he said.

At the end of last year, branches belonging to most of China's top state banks and other financial institutions were fined and criticised for using illegal funds to play the stock markets. ($1 = 8.3 yuan)
